opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to put it is that the local learning coefficient is a measure of model complexity. Roughly, it tells you how many "effective parameters" the model is using at a particular point in parameter space, or more precisely, how fast the volume of nearly-as-good solutions shrinks as you demand lower and lower loss. A low learning coefficient means there's a big, flat, degenerate basin around your solution. Lots of directions you can move without hurting the loss. A high learning coefficient means the solution is more tightly pinned down.

Memorization, intuitively, is expensive in that sense. If you memorize a lookup table of individual data points, each one has to be stored somewhere, and that eats up degrees of freedom. There aren't many ways to perturb the weights without forgetting some of the entries. A general algorithm, by contrast, can often be implemented compactly, and compact implementations tend to come with a lot of degeneracy, which shows up as a lower learning coefficient.

So the rough picture is that memorizing solutions tend to have a higher LLC and generalizing solutions a lower one. That gives you a nice story for things like grokking. Early in training, the model fits the training set by memorizing, and the LLC climbs. Later, it finds a simpler, generalizing solution, and you can actually see the LLC come back down. Bayesian learning is trading off loss against complexity, and once a solution with comparable loss but lower complexity becomes available, it's preferred.

I'd put some caveats on that, though. First, the LLC isn't a memorization detector. It measures complexity, and some genuinely general algorithms are complex. If the task needs a lot of structure, the LLC will reflect that. A larger LLC doesn't automatically mean the model is memorizing, and you should be careful about reading it that way.

Second, it depends on the data distribution you measure against. When you estimate the LLC you're looking at how the loss changes nearby, on some dataset. If you estimate on the training set, you're asking how much complexity the model spends fitting that particular data. You can also do restricted or data-refined versions, measuring the LLC with respect to a subset of data or a subset of the weights. That's where it gets more interesting for memorization questions. You might ask, for example, how much complexity is attributable to specific tokens or examples, and whether that looks like rote storage or something shared across many inputs.

Third, there's a relationship to the generalization side of the theory. In SLT, the learning coefficient appears in the asymptotic expression for the Bayesian generalization error. So, roughly, the more complexity you pay for, the bigger the gap you should expect, at least in the Bayesian setting. That's the formal sense in which "more memorization, worse generalization" connects to the theory. How well that transfers to SGD-trained networks is an empirical question, and we've been trying to probe it.

So my short answer: the LLC is a principled way of counting how much of the model's capacity is being spent, and memorization is one of the main things that spends capacity without buying you generalization. It's a useful lens, but it's a measure of complexity, not a direct readout of memorization.

r001.rationale: The response says the LLC depends on the data distribution used to measure it and distinguishes estimates on the training set from restricted or data-refined estimates.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention attention heads, learned n-grams or multigrams, or an observed positive correlation between them and learning coefficients.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about a fair amount, because the local learning coefficient, the LLC, is often described as a measure of model complexity, and the natural question is: complexity of what? And I think memorization is actually a really clean case for seeing what the LLC is and isn't tracking.

So the way to think about the LLC is that it's measuring how many effective degrees of freedom the model is actually using at a particular point in parameter space. It comes from asymptotic expansions of the Bayesian free energy, but intuitively, it's asking: if I perturb the weights a little bit, how quickly does the loss go up? If there are lots of directions you can move in without changing the loss, the model is in some sense simpler, lower effective dimension, and the LLC is small. If the loss basin is sharp in many directions, the model is using a lot of its parameters and the LLC is larger.

Now, memorization is interesting because when a model memorizes a training example, it's typically carving out a very specific, high-curvature region of the loss landscape. It needs to pin down a bunch of parameters precisely to reproduce that one example, and those parameters aren't doing much else. So memorization tends to show up as an increase in the local learning coefficient. You're spending degrees of freedom on things that don't generalize. Whereas when a model learns a genuine structure, a rule, a circuit that handles an entire class of inputs, it often does so in a way that's more degenerate, more compressible, and you get a lower LLC than you'd expect for the amount of data it's fitting.

And that connects to the generalization side of things, because in SLT the learning coefficient is literally the thing that controls the trade-off between fit and complexity in the free energy. So a model that's memorized will have low training loss but a high LLC, and the free energy, the Bayesian analog of a generalization bound, will penalize that. A model that's found the actual structure will have a comparable training loss but a lower LLC, and the theory says that's the solution that gets favored.

Where it gets subtle is that the LLC is a scalar, so it can't tell you what was memorized or which component of the model is doing it. In practice we've been looking at things like per-data-point or per-component refinements, restricting the estimate to subsets of the data or subsets of the weights, and those start to let you localize. You can ask: which examples contribute most to the increase in complexity? And those tend to be the outliers, the mislabeled examples, the ones the model has no choice but to memorize.

The other caveat is that we're estimating this with SGLD-based sampling, and the estimates are noisy and can be sensitive to hyperparameters. So I wouldn't say we have a crisp theorem that memorization equals LLC going up. It's more that the theory gives you a reason to expect that relationship, and empirically it's held up well in the settings we've looked at, like grokking, where you see the LLC climb during the memorization phase and then drop as the model finds the general solution.

r001.rationale: The response describes estimating the LLC on subsets of the data and asks which examples contribute most to its increase, communicating that the evaluated dataset affects the LLC.

r002.rationale: The response does not report a correlation involving an attention head’s learning coefficient and the number of distinct n-grams or multigrams it learned.

astra-6.text:
I’d be a little careful about identifying the local learning coefficient with memorization directly. The local learning coefficient is a measure of the effective complexity of a model around a particular parameter setting, relative to a particular loss and data distribution. Roughly, it asks how much you have to constrain the parameters to keep the loss close to its minimum. That can be very different from counting the parameters, because many parameter changes might leave the model’s behavior unchanged.

The connection to memorization is that fitting arbitrary details of individual examples generally requires additional independent constraints. If you can explain a thousand examples with one shared rule, that can be a simpler solution than storing a thousand unrelated answers. So you might expect memorization to correspond to a higher local learning coefficient, all else being equal.

But that’s an intuition, not an identification. The coefficient doesn’t tell you which examples were memorized, and it isn’t a count of facts or bits stored in the weights. You also have to specify what distribution you’re measuring it on. A model can behave very differently on its training examples and on new examples. So I’d treat it as a way to investigate the complexity of the mechanism supporting a model’s predictions, rather than as a direct memorization meter.

r001.rationale: The response says the coefficient is relative to a particular data distribution and that you have to specify the distribution on which it is measured.

r002.rationale: The response does not report an observed correlation involving an attention head’s learning coefficient and the number of distinct n-grams or multigrams it learned.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a connection, but I wouldn’t identify the local learning coefficient directly with how much a model has memorized. It’s more a measure of the effective complexity of a solution: how many directions in parameter space are actually constrained by the loss, and how strongly they’re constrained.

The intuition is that if you memorize a bunch of independent facts, you need additional degrees of freedom to fit those facts. Whereas if you discover a rule that explains them together, you can potentially describe the same data with fewer effective degrees of freedom. So you might expect memorizing solutions to have a higher local learning coefficient than solutions that exploit shared structure.

But that’s an intuition, not a general equivalence. The coefficient depends on the model, the data distribution, and the particular region of parameter space you’re looking at. It doesn’t tell you what the model has memorized, or distinguish memorization from generalization on its own. I’d think of it as a way of investigating the complexity associated with those behaviors, rather than a direct measure of memorization.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the coefficient depends on the data distribution, but does not state that it depends on the dataset on which it is evaluated.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not report a positive correlation involving an attention head’s learning coefficient and the number of distinct n-grams or multigrams it learned.
